newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TYSON-HOLYFIELD LOOKS SET FOR NOVEMBER.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TYSON-HOLYFIELD LOOKS SET FOR NOVEMBER.

text.p: Some of the lustre may be off both men now, but Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield, six years later than originally planned, likely will fight on November 9, executives of Showtime cable television said on Friday.
A formal announcement of the fight is expected on Saturday after the Tyson-Bruce Seldon World Boxing Association (WBA) title fight.
Holyfield and Tyson originally were set to fight in 1990. But Tyson injured his ribs and before a new date could be agreed to, he was sent to prison for three years on a rape conviction.
The 33-year-old Holyfield, looking very fit, said he recently had passed a rigorous physical examination at the Mayo Clinic requested by officials of the Nevada State Athletic Commission.
Nevada officials had become concerned about Holyfield's health, especially after two of the former two-time world champion's three fights against Riddick Bowe.
Holyfield, now 32-3, first won the undisputed heavyweight title in 1991 by knocking out James "Buster" Douglas, who had knocked out Tyson the previous year.

But Holyfield lost it on a 12-round decision to Bowe in 1992, and afterwards Holyfield went to the hospital where it was first reported that he had a heart problem. Holyfield retired but changed his mind, saying subsequent tests had invalidated the first diagnosis.
Holyfield fought Bowe again in 1993, winning back two of his three titles on a close decision. Holyfield lost them in 1994 to Michael Moorer.

Holyfield and Bowe fought a third time in 1995 without a title at stake. Bowe survived a knockdown and near knockout in the sixth round when Holyfield, seemingly inexplicably, did not wade in and finish off Bowe, who went on to stop Holyfield in the eighth round.

Holyfield said on Friday he did not move in for the kill in the sixth round because he had been ill in the weeks leading up to the bout, and he was afraid he would not have enough stamina for the rest of the fight if he failed to stop Bowe when he had him hurt.
Holyfield last fought in May when he looked ragged and weak in stopping undersized heavyweight Bobby Czyz in the fifth round.
"My life is not built around one fighter," said Holyfield in denying that a Tyson fight would be a capstone to his career.

"Tyson just happens to be one of the best fighters in my era and I wanted to fight all the great fighters of my era. But we shouldn't compete for just a match, we should fight for a championship," Holyfield said.
"I want to leave with an uplifted spirit, I want to leave as a champion," he said. "I came into this game to be a champion, and I want to leave as a champion."
Tyson, 30, is a 23-1 favourite to beat Seldon to win the WBA title.

Holyfield, one of the most courageous fighters ever and one who never met a brawl he didn't like, grinned a little when asked if he could restrain himself from going toe-to-toe with the powerful Tyson and box him instead.

"I just only do that (brawl) to establish respect," he said, adding that you have to "let your opponent know you're gonna fight him. You gotta do both (box and brawl). You can't beat him unless you do both."
Holyfield said he could knock Tyson down and "when a puncher gets hit he tends to stay down" because he is not used to getting hit hard.
Holyfield was asked his reaction to those who worry about the dangers of fighting the hard-punching Tyson after all of Holyfield's tough fights through the years.
"I have respect for myself. I'm know I'm not going to hurt myself," he said. "I will win because I'm a winner."
